o: Each letter contributes its alphabet position (a=1..z=26) to a score. We ask if some split point i makes score(s[0..i]) equal score(s[i+1..n-1]). In "adcb" the split after "ad" gives 5 = 5, so true; in "bace" no split balances, so false. Since n <= 100 even a brute force works, but a running prefix sum answers in one pass: a split after index i is balanced exactly when 2 * prefix(i) equals the total score.
k: The split condition is prefix(i) = total - prefix(i), i.e. 2*prefix(i) = total.
A single running sum turns the check into O(1) per split point.
Only splits with both sides non-empty are allowed (i from 0 to n-2).

a.i: Recompute both side scores independently for every split index. Perfectly clear and fast enough for n <= 100.
s: Compute score of every prefix and suffix (or recompute per split).
For each i in [0, n-2], compare the two scores.
a.t: O(n^2) - n splits, each rescoring both sides in O(n)

a.i: Accumulate the prefix score while scanning; a valid split exists exactly when the running sum hits half of the total at some interior position.
s: Compute the total score of s.
Scan i from 0 to n-2 adding s[i]'s score to a running sum.
Return true as soon as 2 * running == total; otherwise false.
a.t: O(n) - one pass to total, one pass to scan splits

w: Always present the running-sum version; the brute force is only a warm-up. Pitfalls: allowing an empty side (stop at n-2), off-by-one on the split index, and forgetting 'a' maps to 1 not 0. Follow-up: return the number of valid splits, or handle uppercase/mixed alphabets.
